ANNOUNCEMENT BY MINISTER OF SETTLEMENT OF STRIKE
speechtext:
With your permission, sir, and with the indulgence of the house I should like to make a brief reference to the recently concluded strike by the Canadian brotherhood of locomotive firemen and enginemen on the Canadian Pacific Railway. As hon. members probably are aware by now, the strike has been terminated. Agreement was signed in Montreal last night at 11.59 p.m. by Mr. N. R. Crump, president, on behalf of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and by Mr. John Graham, chairman of the Canadian Pacific branch of the firemen's brotherhood.
The signing of the agreement ended the strike in its third day and followed a series of negotiations which lasted right up to a few moments before the agreement was finally signed. Naturally I was most pleased when finality was reached in a situation which was at best troublesome and contentious and which at worst contained the elements of a far-reaching and serious impasse.
Hon. members are no doubt aware that the problem of the eventual disposition of the diesel firemen on the Canadian Pacific Railway is one which has exercised the close attention of the management of the railway and the representatives of the brotherhood involved, as well as the best efforts of a royal commission and the solicitude of successive governments for more than two years. As Minister of Labour I am happy to be able to report that the settlement which was reached was such that there will be an absolute minimum of dislocation in so far as the personnel involved are concerned.
I feel also that I should like to commend the principals on both sides in the negotiations for the fact that, even in the anxiety and at times heat of the discussions, they were able to keep before them the larger consideration of the general welfare, as well as their own particular interests which were, of course, extensive in this matter. I feel that the settlement which has been achieved is one which has given to both sides as much as could be expected under the circumstances. I feel also that the general welfare has been
served in that the matter has been brought to termination and the spectre of serious difficulty has been averted.
I may add that I was in almost constant communication with negotiants on both sides last evening, and I was most happy to be able to inform the Prime Minister shortly after midnight last night that agreement had been reached.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT BY MINISTER OF SETTLEMENT OF STRIKE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure that we welcome most heartily the announcement that the Canadian Pacific Railway strike has been settled. We know that a railway strike at any time in a nation like ours is a serious matter. We have followed the negotiations, as reports have been appearing in the press, since they began. On the basis of the information we were able to get from the press I believe the settlement is not entirely but very closely in line with the offer made by the Canadian Labour Congress and union on Thursday last. It would seem that if a little extra effort had been made at that time on the part of the other people who were taking part in these three-way conferences, a settlement might then in fact have been reached so the railway strike would not have taken place. As I say, we are pleased that it has been settled; and no matter what has been said in the press to the contrary we think the results show that in Canada we have a very responsible labour movement.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Inquiries of the Ministry
Has the attention of the minister been drawn to the front page report in this morning's Globe and Mail to the effect that the United States Senate internal security subcommittee is reviving the E. Herbert Norman case in a prelude to a full-dress defence of its investigation of our Canadian diplomats, including Mr. Bryce.
If so, is his department contemplating making any representation to the responsible department in Washington, and, should the investigation be proceeded with, will Canada's position be made abundantly clear on this matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to this question I must state at the outset that I have not seen the report which has been prepared pursuant to the direction of that committee of the United States Senate. All I can depend on are the newspaper reports. Assuming that these are accurate I must say that I resent an additional occurrence of ex parte proceedings, leaving behind innuendos against Canadian citizens.
For example: I have known Mr. Bryce for a long time and I have a high regard for him. According to this morning's newspaper he made the statement that he has nothing to hide, and I endorse that statement on behalf of Mr. Bryce.
One aspect of this matter concerns my department. Hon. members will recall that on April 10 last year our ambassador in Washington, acting on the instructions of the Canadian government, presented a note to the United States government regarding the procedures which had been followed intermittently by the internal security subcommittee, a subcommittee of a committee of the United States Senate, in releasing the names of Canadians who had been mentioned in its proceedings and particularly in its executive sessions. I am going to take the time of the house to read a part of that note:
The Canadian government has more than once complained of the methods employed by that subcommittee in releasing the names of Canadians and has stated that if the names of Canadian officials appear in evidence before investigating committees in Washington, those names should be sent in confidence to the Canadian government so that the allegations can be investigated and dealt with in Canada.
This procedure requested by the Canadian government has, however, never been followed and references made in proceedings of the subcommittee to individual Canadians have not been made known to the Canadian government except through the press.
As the United States government knows, the Canadian government finds the procedures adopted by the subcommittee with respect to Canadians difficult to understand, unfair and indeed intolerable. The Canadian government therefore requests

Inquiries of the Ministry again that these procedures be altered in so far as Canadians are concerned along the lines indicated above.
In reply to this request the United States Secretary of State, in a note dated August 13, 1957 stated:
The view of your government was made known to the appropriate members of the United States congress, at which time the Department of State emphasized the great importance the United. States attaches to maintaining the friendliest relations with the government of Canada. I wish to assure you that this sentiment is wholeheartedly entertained by the congress.
In view of the friendly sentiments expressed in this way by the United States congress the Canadian government decided to let the matter rest, trusting that should the names of Canadian citizens thereafter appear in evidence before congressional investigating committees these names would, as we had suggested, be sent to us in confidence for investigation if necessary in Canada.
The developments to which the hon. member has referred have shown that this trust was misplaced. Once again an investigating committee of the United States congress has made public the name of a Canadian civil servant in complete disregard of the Canadian government's views forcibly made known to the congress only a few months ago as to the fair and proper way to deal with matters of this kind. I am sure that all hon. members of this house will share the Canadian government's disappointment at this turn of events. I am, therefore, instructing our ambassador in Washington to convey to the United States government the sense of the statement I have just made.

Mr. Speaker, may I direct a supplementary question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but before doing so I wish to state I am certain that all hon. members appreciate the information that has been given to us by the minister. However, in view of what he said and in view of the question of the Norman case being reopened and a new name brought in, could I ask the minister if it is now the intention of his department to again make the strongest possible protest to Washington and to make our Canadian position exceedingly well known, not only in the interests of diplomacy but in defence of the two men who have been named in this fashion?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the house will agree that this is not supplementary but a repetition of a question which has already been answered.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO PROTECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this question. The answer is as follows. I have had detailed discussions with a delegation from the Canadian Metal Mining Association on the subject of the possible reimposition by the United States of a tax on copper. Copper is normally subject to a United States import tax of 2 cents per pound, but in recent years this import tax has been temporarily suspended by act of congress. According to this legislation the suspension will end on June 30 next. The United States administration has not seen fit at this time to seek a renewal of this suspension, which has been so obviously in the interests of both Canada and the United States. In accordance with commitments under our trade agreement, the United States rate of import tax on copper will, in the absence of further suspension, amount to either 1.7 cents or 2 cents per pound, depending on whether the market price in the United States is above or below 24 cents per pound.
Hon. members may be assured that the views of the Canadian government as to the importance of ensuring that there is no increased tariff or other barrier to exports of base metals from Canada to the United States have been made known to the United States government.

He said: Mr. Chairman, may I, as the first member of the house to address you since you have assumed the office of Deputy Speaker of the house and chairman of its committees, extend to you the heartiest congratulations and warmest good wishes for your success in the important responsibilities which you have assumed. You hold this office by a decision of the house and in due

recognition of your own high personal merit. In addition however, sir, I know it is a matter of very considerable gratification to all hon. members in this house that in your election to this high office, a worthy son is following in the footsteps of a very worthy and distinguished father.
I am sure it will be the wish of all hon. members that in the discharge of your responsibilities you will earn the same confidence and the same gratitude that your distinguished father earned in his time in the discharge of these same duties 40 years ago.
As all hon. members are aware, Mr. Chairman, from the statement I made to the house yesterday, the house is being asked today to vote a fraction of the estimates which were tabled yesterday for the fiscal year 1958-59. The expenses of the government have been already provided for only until the 16th day of May, which is Friday of this week, and the government will be without funds after that date. The government has taken the utmost steps to ensure under the existing circumstances the utmost control by the house over the appropriation of needed moneys.
By way of emphasizing the urgency of today's motion, may I remind the house that in addition to the fact that funds available now will be exhausted after May 16, it is always necessary for the treasury to have funds in hand some days before the date on which the salary and pay cheques go out because they have to be sent to all parts of the country. We have to allow time as well for passing by the Senate and royal assent to the bill.
The house is concerned as to the extent of the funds to be appropriated under the present measure. The appropriation now proposed is intended to provide funds for the needs of the government until the 31st day of May. That means that a further request for interim supply will be made to the house in the first week of June. It is, of course, obvious that we might have asked for a larger sum now, but we felt that under all the circumstances the usual course should be followed of asking in the first motion for interim supply the equivalent of two months' needs.
There are some hundreds of items in the book of estimates tabled yesterday. In all but 42 cases the sum now asked for is one-sixth of the total, or in other words the equivalent of two months of these items which are capable of being disbursed or lend themselves to disbursement on a pro rata basis throughout the year. As to the 42 items in question, they fall within one or other of the four categories I mentioned yesterday of 57071-3-5J
Interim Supply
cases in which the needs contemplated by the item are not capable of pro rata calculation or disbursement month by month throughout the year.
The total amount the house is being asked to provide for these needs to May 31 appears as the sum of $626,292,380.09. But that sum is subject to a reduction in a manner I shall mention in a moment. I wish to make it very clear that even in the case of these 42 items, in none of them is the house asked to vote today the entire sum. There are a few of them in which the program is already well advanced and in which as much as eleven-twelfths of the total item are asked today, but these are items of an exceptional nature. I stress the fact that at least a portion of these extraordinary items remains to be voted by the house on a future occasion. Therefore with respect thereto the house will retain its full opportunity to discuss, review and consider. I shall shortly be giving to the house the usual assurance with respect to the rights of all hon. members of the house in reference to every one of the items of which a portion is being appropriated today.
I mentioned yesterday the issuance of two special warrants under the terms of the Financial Administration Act by His Excellency the Governor General on the advice of council in order to meet the needs of government from April 1 until the 16th day of May. These are the two warrants which are referred to in the proviso which constitutes the closing paragraph of the resolution now under discussion. The two warrants for which I gave particulars yesterday amount to the sum of $303,560,195. Every item that was included in the governor general's warrants is to be found in the book of estimates tabled yesterday with one exception, and one only, which I mentioned yesterday. That is an item of $7 million appropriated by governor general's warrant which does not find its way into the book of estimates because it is a loan to Trans-Canada Air Lines and therefore will be included in due course in the bill that normally provides for the requirements of the Canadian National Railways.
That item of $7 million which was appropriated by governor general's warrant carries the needs of Trans-Canada Air Lines to June 30, and it is trusted that by that time the house will have been in a position to pass the bill respecting the provision for Canadian National Railways financing. So with regard to all items in the governor general's warrants, with that one exception they are to be found in the book of estimates which was tabled yesterday and a portion of each item in which the house is being asked to appropriate today.

Interim Supply
A question may be asked as to what is the appropriate relationship of the appropriation already made by those two governor general's warrants to the appropriation of a portion of these items in the estimates which the house is being asked to approve today. There was a similar situation in the year 1940. There had been an election in the month of March of that year. The house was called to meet in May on a date a little later than the date on which the present parliament was called to meet. Both in the late days of the fiscal year ended March 31, 1940 and in the period of April and May 1940 prior to the convening of parliament a number of governor general's warrants had been issued. Indeed, the number was quite formidable; actually fifteen warrants had been issued. In the fiscal year which had commenced April 1, 1940 the warrants issued in that period had appropriated sums aggregating approximately $100 million; and I am sure that the finance minister at that time, the late lamented Mr. Ralston, was faced with a similar question.
One finds that in the first appropriation bill that he introduced in the early days of the 1940 session the house was called upon to appropriate sums intended to provide all needed supply for the first two months of the year, but in the bill no provision was made respecting the governor general's warrants which had already taken effect and which by their nature had already appropriated sums of money.
The first interim supply or the first appropriation bill of that session made no reference whatever to the governor general's warrants. We have considered that the better practice is to ask the house in this first appropriation by statute in this new session to take note of the issuance of the two governor general's warrants since the opening of this present fiscal year on April 1.
What about the earlier one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the practice which was followed on that occasion is the one which had obtained earlier and it is our view, Mr. Chairman, that the course which the government now proposes is one which preserves more directly the control of the house over the appropriation of public money. In other words perhaps I might say this; that in 1940 on the first motion for interim supply the subject of the governor general's warrants was not even mentioned. The interim supply was voted through all stages in this house in a matter of about eight or nine minutes and it was only in the final supply bill of the year that account was taken of the sums which had already

been appropriated by governor general's warrant prior to the opening of the session.
The next appropriation by way of interim supply on July 31, 1940 occupies half a column in Hansard, indicating that the motion was passed through all stages in perhaps a minute or a minute and a half, but in the final appropriation of the year reference was made to the governor general's warrants and I should like to lay before the house the clause in question. The statute is chapter 47 of the statute of 1940, and clause 2 of that statute provides for the appropriation of the named sum of money and then proceeds to set forth this proviso:
Provided the amount hereby authorized to be paid and applied in respect to each item, set forth in said schedule A, shall be deemed to include and not to be in addition to, the amount authorized for each such item by governor general's warrants issued during the fiscal year 1940-41 prior to the 16th day of May, 1940.
We propose that the measure which the house is being asked to pass today should include a clause in those words so that it will be clearly understood, and indeed is expressly provided, both in the resolution now under discussion and in the bill to follow, that the house is being asked to appropriate the full sum of $626 million odd, which is the entire sum required to meet the expenses of government from April 1 to May 31, and there will be a provision that this sum is to be deemed to include and not to be in addition to the two sums already appropriated by governor general's warrants. In saying that I ask hon. members to bear in mind, of course, that under the-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

It would not be proper to ask the house to reappropriate sums already appropriated; nevertheless we are anxious that in the fullest manner the control and authority of the house over appropriation and expenditure of moneys should be clearly asserted, and that is why both the resolution and the bill take the form I have indicated.

I would now like to say a word or two about the rights of the house with respect to discussion and approval or disapproval of items under these estimates at a later period in the session. All these items in the book of estimates will be reviewed, of course, in the ordinary way in the committee of supply, department by department. Neither the appropriation of any item by governor general's warrant nor the appropriation of any portion of any item by an interim supply bill will prejudice the right of hon. members to discuss such an item when it is reached in the ordinary course in committee of supply. The position in that respect is not in any degree different with respect to those items appropriated by the governor general's warrants from the position of those items appropriated by interim supply. Never has a vote of interim supply nor an appropriation by governor general's warrant precluded the fullest discussion of the item when it is reached in committee of supply in the ordinary course.
What about February 1?

Mr. Chairman,

I would remind the house also that parliament has been called to meet at the earliest possible date after the election, indeed, two days too early for one hon. member; that

It was peculiarly fitting that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should make a statement today on the Premium Iron Ores case. This is the topic that I planned to deal with, and it happens that this statement is one more of the peculiarities connected with this strange and interesting case which I plan to review rather thoroughly. I shall conclude with some questions.
The peculiarities, so far as I am concerned, begin with the fact that I find myself arguing along the same lines as such reactionary institutions, in my view, as the Toronto Globe and Mail. Aside from that, this Premium Iron Ores case has a great deal of interest for me and my area. If this test case should be won by the United States government it could affect a great number of corporations operating in my constituency. The case, in essence, is one brought in the United States tax court against Premium Iron Ores, the sales agency for Steep Rock iron, and two United States citizens, the charge being that their company and they, themselves, were liable for taxation in the United States, even though we have a convention with the United States to avoid double taxation, and even though these men and the company paid their taxes in Canada.
Steep Rock iron mine presents a very interesting story, beginning in 1939. It was really begun by people from the city of Port Arthur. They found three very large high grade deposits of iron underneath a large lake. In order to get the mine under way they required a considerable amount of capital. Unfortunately they were not able to raise that in Canada. In 1940 they approached two Cleveland financiers, Cyrus Eaton and Frank Daley, and they began inquiries as to whether or not they could get United States capital through this particular group. In July, 1942, Mr. Eaton undertook to raise $7.5 million, to provide a program, to look after relationships with the federal and provincial governments, and to work out a sales system for Steep Rock iron ore.
On September 11, 1942, the Department of National Revenue, income tax division, issued the following ruling so far as the general setup and financing of Steep Rock iron mine and Premium iron ores were concerned:
The setup re financing as contained in the memorandum of September 8, 1942, is aceptable and no tax will arise against any entity by reason of the fact that 2 million shares of the company are valued at one cent a share on the books of the sales company.

With regard to the position of the sales company under the Excess Profits Tax Act, the ruling was:
"The sales company will be exempt from tax for the same period as the operating company and will be allowed the same rate of depletion on net profits realized. In effect, this means that the rate of taxation of the sales company will be the same as that of the operating company."
In other words, both Steep Rock and Premium Iron Ores, the sales company, were exempt for three years from taxation dating from the day operations were commenced.
That is a point to remember in connection with this case. Mr. Eaton, working as the head of an investment house and also as the United States citizen most interested in putting Steep Rock into production, managed to get the Canadian government to undertake the building of a spur line and construction of a dock at Port Arthur. The total expenditure by the government was $2.5 million. He managed to get the Ontario hydro to undertake an expenditure of $1.5 million to instal hydro lines. This group managed to get an agency of the United States government, Reconstruction Finance Corporation

rather ironically this institution was begun by that free enterpriser, President Herbert Hoover, and yet we find it taking this rather socialistic attitude-to lend $5 million to this Canadian company to get it under way. The whole approach required the co-operation of the United States government, the Canadian government and the provincial government. They were all closely intertwined, and the conclusion one may come to is that the Canadian government at the time and the United States government at the time were interested in seeing this mine in operation. Of course, if you look at the year, 1942, you can understand why.
The tax convention to avoid double taxation was brought up to date a year before the arrangements were completed for the start of Steep Rock iron mine through this $5 million loan from Reconstruction Finance Corporation. The mine experienced considerable difficulty during its early operations largely due to flooding and the spreading of silt, but it finally managed to get going fairly well in 1944-45.	[DOT]
By the end of the war it was recognized as one of the premium propositions. Indeed it was sort of the great leader of iron ore operations in Canada. The company was accepted as a Canadian company, Steep Rock Iron Mines. So was its sales agency. It was being taxed in Canada. Both of them were being taxed in Canada. Things went along in that way until 1947 when something occurred owing to a peculiarity of the United States tax system. I should not say a peculiarity; it is part of their law and we 57071-3-6i
Interim Supply
must respect it. They have a provision in their tax code that anyone that is able to present the gist of an idea as an informer to the tax authorities which leads to conviction and collection of taxes and penalty is able to collect up to 25 per cent of the penalty and the taxation collected.
What happened in this particular case was that in 1947 an informer came forward to the United States taxing authorities, laying information against Premium Iron Ores, arguing that because they did not have to pay taxes for those first three years under the Canadian tax arrangement the United States government should come in and tax the company for those years because the company happened to have at the head of it, men who had offices in Cleveland. The claim was not asserted until 1953. In other words, from 1947 to 1953 the claim seems to have been under investigation. I think you will recognize that is a very long period. It certainly is of perhaps more than incidental interest that the claim was not proceeded with until the United States government changed at the beginning of 1953. When the claim was proceeded with, it was recognized, of course, that Canada was involved and out of the general discussions came the information that the Canadian authorities had cooperated very fully with the United States authorities. We have the word of one of the witnesses at the tax trial, referring to this period when the investigation was taking place in Canada. The agent concerned said this:
So far as I know, there has never been a prior instance where a revenue agent secured the assistance of a foreign government in assessing tax liability. I met with the director of national revenue and his subordinates. They assigned a Canadian assessor to work with me. Whatever information was available to the assessor was in turn furnished to me. We called on the Royal Bank of Canada and the Canadian assessor asked the manager of the bank to produce records pertaining to Premium Iron Ores Limited. The Toronto investigation took a period of seven months.
That is the end of the quotation from the testimony of this United States agent in the court. We happen to know that that investigation lasted for more than seven months and covered such places as far apart as Winnipeg and Nova Scotia. All through this period before a charge had been laid in United States courts, before a claim was asserted, Canadian officials were co-operating with United States officials in connection with a company that at that particular time was paying taxes in Canada as a Canadian company. The justification for this co-operation is something that we cannot understand very clearly at the present time. The

Interim Supply
Canadian government of course, had representations. For example, they had this representation from the local of the United Steelworkers of America and Steep Rock Lake, Ontario. It was sent to Hon. Milton F. Gregg, Hon. Walter Harris and Hon. Lester B. Pearson. This resolution condemns the role played by Canada in co-operating with the United States authorities. One of the phrases used in the resolution reads as follows:
Whereas, the United States taxing authorities are harassing Consolidated Premium Iron Ores Limited, a Canadian corporation, by claiming taxes from it based on transactions which the Canadian taxing authorities have either taxed or specifically exempted from tax, and
Whereas, we do not believe that it is in the best interest of the employees of Steep Rock Iron Mines Limited, the local community or the economy of Ontario and Canada for United States taxing authorities to harass a Canadian corporation by claiming taxes on Canadian income which have been specifically exempted from tax by the Canadian government.
The concern expressed by such organizations, unions, by representatives of the company, finally led to the government on November 28 of 1956 presenting an aide-memoire from the Canadian ambassador to the Secretary of State. I have checked up on the definition of an aide-memoire and it appears it is used in situations where very powerful but at the same time informal presentation of opinion is given to the foreign country to whom the memoire is sent. The gist of this aide-memoire from the Canadian ambassador to the Secretary of State is in the last paragraph:
The Canadian government, therefore, feel that the United States government should not take from the assistance it obtained from Canadian officials the inference that Canada supports this claim to tax the company because, on the contrary, it is felt that the facts show that when the Canadian government, as a war measure to increase essential production, agreed to exempt this company from income and excess profits tax for a period of three years, it was not contemplated that there would be any United States tax applicable to these operations of the company which the Canadian and the United States governments were both trying to accelerate in the joint interest of the two countries.
In other words this aide-memoire sent to the Canadian ambassador by our prime minister of 1956 covers almost exactly the same argument put forward by the resolution that I have read from the union on the scene of Steep Rock Iron Mines. The peculiar effect of this aide-memoire is this. One would tend to think that this would make a strong impression on the United States authorities and might even lead to their decision not to proceed. But we find this:
Under date of December 20, 1956, the Department of State in Washington stated in writing to the foreign affairs committee, as follows:

The effect of the Premium Iron Ores tax case on our international relations with Canada is, of course, a matter of concern to the state department. You may be interested, therefore, in the Canadian official response to the action.
In preparing the United States case, our internal revenue officials received the co-operation of Canadian officials. Throughout this period of preparation and co-operation, no formal representation or objection was made by the Canadian government.
On May 26th, shortly before the case was to be tried, the Canadian ambassador discussed it with the acting secretary of state. During his interview, the ambassador emphasized he had not been instructed to make representations of any kind.
On November 29, 1956, the Canadian ambassador-
At the same time this aide-memoire was given to the United States State Department.
-left with the department of state an aide-memoire on the subject.
Since the Canadian government has not sought representation in connection with the case, either before or after it was brought to the court, the department of state has had no reason to take further action in this regard.
In other words, despite what we may think of the force of this aide-memoire which was dispatched by the former prime minister the department of state advised the United States foreign affairs committee that really this was in effect no representation at all.
The next point in connection with this case developed when the government changed hands. Of course, with a new government in Canada representations were made to this government to take up this case and to stop what in effect could be double taxation if it was successful. On December 23, 1957 the Canadian charge d'affaires delivered a statement to the U.S. secretary of state as follows:
The Canadian government Is desirous of avoiding any misapprehension concerning its position in this matter. Accordingly, the Canadian government would wish the United States government to be aware that the views contained in the aide-memoire presented by the Canadian embassy on November 28, 1956 and in the statement made by the previous Prime Minister in the Canadian House of Commons on April 9, 1957 are very strongly shared by the present Canadian government. For reference purposes the relevant extract from the House of Commons debates for April 9, 1957 is attached.
This extract deals with the question put by the hon. member for Kamloops to the minister of national revenue at that time, the Hon. J. J. McCann, and to the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, who was prime minister at that time, and the substance of this interjection is contained in Mr. St. Laurent's last remark as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the position was taken that there was a question of fact that was now submitted to the court, and if as a consequence of the court's finding on the evidence relating to that question of fact it was felt that the real intent of the treaty with respect to the avoidance of double taxation was not being carried out, there would have to be reconsideration of its terms.

I think it will be agreed that that sounds very much like the statement which was read today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
This was the representation made by the present government on December 23, 1957. The next date which is of any interest in this case is when the United States tax court came out with its decision. The judge filed his decision on April 23, 1957 and the petitioners, that is to say Premium Iron Ores Limited, Mr. Eaton and Mr. Daley won their case and the interesting thing about this whole judgment is that it is built around the fact that it is not right for the United States tax authorities to proceed against this company because of the tax convention and the protocol between the United States and Canada. In other words we have a United States judge standing up for Canada's position as far as this treaty and the tax convention are concerned and so the judge ruled against the United States tax authorities. The tax authorities thereupon appealed to the whole body of judges of the tax court who ruled against the United States tax authorities. Since then it has been indicated that the United States tax authorities are going to take this case to an appellate court and there is an indication that if they lose there they are going to take it to the supreme court.
That possibility raises an interesting point. If they do take it to the supreme court and should win, as I understand the position from Americans, that means that it has the force of law and no further appeals are available. It also means the penalties must be applied to these two people and to the company and that raises the question that if this should happen will our Canadian authorities then reimburse this company and reimburse these men for the taxes which have been paid in Canada in connection with these operations?
There is, however, a much more interesting point because we hear today from the Secretary of State for External Affairs that on February 28 the United States state department asked the Canadian government what the Minister of National Revenue meant on February 1 when he made a statement in this house in connection with Premium Iron Ores Limited. In effect his statement was that this present government stood behind Mr. St. Laurent's aide-memoire. The statement read by the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that in the course of clarifying observations the Canadian government took the opportunity to review the considerations on which their decision in this matter had been based, and what the minister had in mind in his answer to a question was that the
Interim Supply
Canadian government would wish in due course to study the court of appeal judgment in relation to the facts in the case as to whether the terms of our double taxation convention have been interpreted in the sense we intended them to have at the time when they were indicated and, if not, to consider whether these terms require revision.
We have this relatively strong statement on the position of the Minister of National Revenue, saying in effect that the Canadian government treats this matter very seriously and that it may undertake a complete revision of the double taxation policy, then on March 27, 1958-that is a month after the Canadian government made this representation-we find the United States internal revenue service stating in a letter to the senate committee on foreign affairs-the top officials of the United States revenue department

that J. G. McEntyre, the Canadian deputy minister of national revenue, had agreed with the position taken by the United States. We are not exactly sure as to what is that position with which Mr. McEntyre agreed but we do have the peculiar situation where, before a tax claim is even asserted, United States tax officials through the advice of our Canadian tax officials are being allowed to examine the books and go into the banks and look at the records of many people in this country, people who are actually Canadian citizens. This is something, of course, which our party has been bringing forward for a number of years in order to make income tax records more open and yet we find that our bill is always voted down and it is said that that would be a tremendous violation of Canadian personal freedom. Yet we find that United States tax snoopers can come up here and spend extensive periods of intensive investigation and they seem to be encouraged by Canadian tax officials.
Furthermore, we now have a statement dated one month after our present government has stated it takes a very serious view of the matter to the effect that our Canadian deputy minister of national revenue has agreed with the position taken by the United States.
I have to agree, in fairness to the deputy minister, that we do not know the position the United States has taken, but it seems that it could very easily be the position that these companies, with United States' capital operating in Canada at present, which are taxed by the Canadian government, can also be taxed in certain cases by the United States government. If this is so it is a very serious situation and its seriousness is exemplified by the tremendous number of editorials one reads in such sterling right wing

Interim. Supply
papers as, the Financial Post, the Winnipeg Tribune and the Montreal Gazette.
I would therefore like to suggest to the ministers concerned that they give us some information on the position really taken by their government at the present time in connection with this matter. Do they not think that this has been an invasion of Canadian sovereignty; do they not think it peculiar that the state department receives an aide-memoire through our external affairs department which states something very strongly and at the same time we have another leak to the United States through our Department of National Revenue into the United States treasury which seems to operate completely to one side? There appears to be a lack of rapport in this whole case as between the Department of External Affairs and the Department of National Revenue.
One thing I think we need to know is whether the Canadian government will consider reimbursing these people for taxes already deducted if double taxation does come into effect as the result of the position taken by the United States appeal or supreme court. I think this is something which is quite important because it is, in essence, a test case. 1 do not feel at all ashamed in bringing it forward because I believe it will have a very serious effect on the operations of the particular corporations involved in my part of the country. At the present time Steep Rock Iron Mines is not having an easy time of it; we are losing miners from the Atikokan community and there is not as much ore as possible being shipped. The blow to that company and to its sales agencies from an adverse decision could be extremely serious and could even lead to a shutting down of the mine. I think, therefore, that this is a case which deserves an explanation from the Minister of National Revenue as to the part played in the negotiations by the officials of his own department.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to assure the Minister of Finance that we are doing all we possibly can to expedite the passage of interim supply; I will attempt to say as little as I feel needs to be said.
We in this group were very pleased indeed at the assurance which the minister gave yesterday that time would be allowed later for a full discussion of the remaining estimates of the 1957-58 fiscal year and, especially, for a discussion of the issuing of Governor General's warrants. We are very pleased indeed at the new attitude which the Minister of Finance has adopted since this matter was last taken up in the house on February 1. I can assure him we shall have some very serious considerations to bring forward at that time.

I was a little amused at the reference made by the spokesman for the Liberal party on the size of the estimates for the year 1958-59. We in our group have long realized that the population and the problems of Canada are growing and that the responsibilities of government have to grow along with them. When we consider the change in the value of money we have never been particularly surprised or horrified to find we are confronted with a growing gross national expenditure. I must, however, point out at this time that though the government's expenditures are obviously increasing there is some suspicion that the government's gross income may be declining. For the federal government that is not an overly serious matter because the dominion government has at its disposal ways and means of operating on an income which is less than its expenditure. I am referring to the principle of deficit financing, and many indications have already been given that we may have to meet a very heavy outlay by this means.
I should like to refer now to some of the expenditures which the Minister of Finance makes and which are, I believe, made directly by his department, namely the assistance given to another level of government, municipal government. The assessment notices from municipalities, in our province at least, are now being mailed to homeowners, and our people back home are going to view with some concern the growing expenditures of the federal government and the growing costs of municipal government. They will realize that while the federal government has ways and means of meeting such growing expenditures in a time of recession their local municipal government has no such easy, or comparatively easy, remedy. The only remedy available to municipal governments is to add to an already high tax burden on Canadian homes, Canadian farms and other Canadian real estate. The situation which exists in my own province applies, I think, throughout Canada. It is very serious indeed, and unless some action is forthcoming shortly to provide relief -and I do not say that the federal government alone is responsible, because some, at least of the provincial governments should be able to do more-we may one of these days be faced with a mass resignation of our municipal elected officers throughout the nation and I am sure none of us would like to see that happen.
I call to mind again, as I have done before in this house, what the Minister of Finance and his colleagues in the government had to say on this subject when they were members of the opposition. I do not wish to delay the committee too much, but I must read again

one sentence by the present Minister of Finance as reported on page 4788 of Hansard, of May 17, 1954:
The federal government, with its abundant sources, should be devising ways of helping the municipalities to meet these urgent demands for necessary but costly services which they are financially unable to provide.
And on page 4789 he said:
There must be, in my submission, an opening of the eyes of the federal government to the way in which they are increasing the burdens and the difficulties of the municipalities.
And the Minister without Portfolio, then the hon. member for Greenwood, on the same day, at page 4786, said:
It is no answer to shrug off the municipalities.
I was very pleased indeed to learn that on February 7 last during the election campaign, six days after dissolution, the municipalities of Canada presented a brief to the federal cabinet. I understand from the newspaper reports that the cabinet listened to the brief for 90 minutes, and that subsequently there were several announcements. I wish to refer to what is possibly the most important announcement, as reported in the Gazette, datelined Ottawa, February 7. This is a Canadian Press dispatch reading.
Prime Minister Diefenbaker said today he plans to call an informal federal-municipal conference this year to discuss the financial plight of Canadian municipalities.
That indicated a slight change of heart, because last fall we pleaded with the Minister of Finance to admit municipalities to a dominion-provincial conference, and the most we could get out of him was an agreement that they might attend as observers. Later on in the session he said: "We respect the constitution", indicating that there was something in the British North America Act which might prevent the federal government from holding serious discussions with municipal governments. I am very pleased that the Prime Minister, as reported in the Globe and Mail of February 8, announced at the same time that he planned to call for a new deal in financing at a dominion-provincial-municipal conference, and I am very pleased to say that he has now found room under the British North America Act to call it, unless he was wrongly reported, a dominion-provincial-municipal conference. In any event, the Prime Minister said, he planned to hold a dominion-municipal conference before 1959. Our newspapers out west said the Prime Minister had promised to hold an informal dominion-municipal conference.
The reason I am raising this matter at this time is because I notice in the speech from the throne only a claim that the government has helped municipalities, meaning I
Interim Supply
suppose that they have done so by helping provincial governments. But there is nothing in the speech from the throne to indicate that the Minister of Finance or the government have any serious intention of implementing any early action to increase the aid which they plan to give to municipal governments.
At the conference between the municipalities and the cabinet on February 7 the following point was raised as reported in the Gazette of February 8:
Pending a permanent solution of the problems of municipalities the federal government should take interim measures to assist municipal governments.
I realize that that is not an easy matter. The problem involves our whole constitutional arrangement. I am keenly interested in this matter and have pointed out the needs of the municipal governments in this house for a number of years. I would like to point out to the minister that we have operated under the British North America Act for some 91 years. In many respects and especially with regard to those aspects that apply to financial resources of municipal governments the British North America Act belongs to the horse and buggy days.
In nine years we will be observing our one hundredth anniversary as a nation. I appeal to the minister to use his influence to arrange a dominion-provincial-municipal constitutional conference which would . explore the possibilities of finding agreement between the various regions of Canada, the diversified interests of Canada and the several levels of government in Canada so that at an early date and not later than our one hundredth anniversary we might be able to announce a new constitutional arrangement which would supply adequate resources to those levels of government that are charged with the heaviest responsibilities of government.
It is very easy for us in our ivory tower here to claim that we need over $6,000 million a year to run this government. It is relatively simple to find ways and means to obtain the money that we intend to spend.
I have yet to find a government that thinks any of its expenditures could reasonably be reduced. However, I plead with the government to acknowledge that this is the time to indicate to those of our people who are active in the real business of making democracy work on the home front, these willing public spirited citizens who sacrifice much more of themselves in the common welfare than many of us do as members of the federal house, that relief will be provided. Let us not wait for some possible future dominion-provincial conference to reach a solution which will be an interim

Interim Supply
solution at best because most of these agreements operate for only five-year periods.
I hope the minister will offer the municipal governments some hope and encouragement at an early date and will not say to us again at some future time, "We respect the constitution," because it has been pointed out over the years by many of us in this house and also by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities in its briefs that the Minister of Finance could relieve the financial plight of our municipalities in many ways without violating even the spirit of the British North America Act.
I wish the minister would say at this time what the government has in mind when it refers to a dominion-provincial-municipal conference and also what it has in mind when it refers to an informal dominion-municipal conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have just a brief word to say. First of all I should like to extend to my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River my personal congratulations on his selection as financial critic of the official opposition and say that I know his experience with the Department of Finance will enable him to render to the house and to the official opposition very high service in that capacity. I have already indicated indirectly to him that the services of the department are at his disposal to supply any factual information he may require at any time in the discharge of his responsibilities.'
May I thank the minister for that courtesy already given earlier today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to deal at length with the various matters touched on by the hon. gentlemen who have spoken. In the case of most of their comments which were of a financial nature I believe the budget or the stage of consideration of the items themselves in committee of supply in due course would be a better place to do so.
With respect to the dominion-provincial conference I think that is a matter on which my friend the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam should address his inquiry to the Prime Minister.

Mr. Chairman, I want to take this opportunity to bring a matter to the attention of the house which is of serious concern to the people of southeastern British Columbia. As hon. members who have been here for a number of years know I never raise a matter unless it is one of public importance and necessary at the time. Also I might say I promised a lot of organizations and people in southeastern British Columbia, including

people in Kootenay West, Kootenay East and in the Okanagan valley, that I would raise this matter in the house at the first opportunity and that is why I do so now.
The question which concerns me is that of the reduction of passenger train service between Vancouver and Medicine Hat by the Canadian Pacific railway commencing this year. It has caused a great deal of concern to business and people generally throughout the whole area. This train service serves a rich and productive area which last year produced in the neighbourhood of $300 million worth of goods. It is the centre of a large coal, mining, smelting and lumbering industry. The interesting aspect of this matter is that this is one of the wealth producing areas of the Canadian Pacific railway. As a matter of fact I wish the Minister of Transport were here because I would say for his information that in my area he is now being referred to by many people as the minister of diminishing transport.
The C.P.R. owns 51 per cent of the stock of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company right in the very area where people are being denied at the present time satisfactory passenger train service from which the railway makes a large percentage of its net profit. For many years we have had a highly satisfactory passenger train service running between Vancouver and Medicine Hat, a first-class train carrying sleeping and dining cars, coaches, baggage and mail cars and so on. It was viewed favourably and supported by people throughout the area but since the beginning of the year the Canadian Pacific railway has installed what is known as a Budd car service which consists of one car with a single engineer in the cab. It has the advantage that it does make an excellent connection with trains Nos. 2 and 3 to Medicine Hat, but it has many other disadvantages. I think what the people are asking for is not unreasonable and that is why I have no hesitation in bringing their representations to the house.
This matter has been discussed at chambers of commerce meetings. All the chambers of commerce in the whole southeastern area of British Columbia have taken very strong exception to this reduction in passenger service. It has been discussed by farmers, organizations, by municipal councils and by all the trade unions in the area. I think I can truthfully say that not only all these organizations but 100 per cent of the people of the southeastern area of British Columbia object very much to being served with this Budd car service at this time. It is a long train journey from Vancouver to Medicine Hat or even to Nelson. It is an overnight journey whichever

way you go and it is a great discomfort to older people because there is no place to lie down. It is a great discomfort to people with families and to children. I have travelled on the train. It is most uncomfortable indeed to have to sit up overnight and suffer that inconvenience, 'particularly to those who are old, people with children and persons who are ill. In addition to that the meal service is very poor indeed. You have to get a sandwich and a cup of coffee from a newsboy. On several occasions even the supplies of food have completely run out before the train reached Vancouver. It is a most inadequate service for a wealth-producing area such as the southeastern portion of British Columbia.
In addition, there are certain other disadvantages. Our country cannot be satisfactorily served by air every day in the winter. During 1957 the planes that were supposed to land at Castlegar were unable to land for something over 80 days. That presents quite a problem to persons who have to go to the coast, persons who are ill and things of that sort. I wish to read a letter which was written by the chairman of the board of the Kootenay lake general hospital. This gentleman was a former official of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. The letter is addressed to the board of transport commissioners for Canada, Ottawa, Ontario, and is dated April 28, 1958. It reads:
Gentlemen:
At the last meeting of the board of directors of the Kootenay lake general hospital, the matter of the passenger train service here was of concern to members, and a resolution was unanimously passed protesting the inadequacy of the present train service, and asking that the board of transport commissioners be notified of this protest, and informed that the lack of service is an obstacle in the way of good patient care.
As you know, train service to and from Nelson is presently confined to a twice-weekly service westward with stopover at Penticton, and a daily service to and from the east. Both these services are day coach only with no separate or private accommodation of any kind.
At fairly frequent intervals it becomes necessary for patients from this hospital to be transported to other facilities-usually at the coast. These patients are sometimes mentally disturbed, sometimes urgent accident cases, sometimes suffering from a communicable disease. In nearly all cases privacy and quiet are recommended conditions for their travelling comfort and well-being. In the case of communicable disease, of course, privacy is a necessity for the protection of other travellers. Recently a patient suffering from a communicable disease had to be taken to the coast by private car as no other means of transportation was available.
Air transport is an alternative for accident cases when weather conditions are favourable, but neither mentally ill persons nor those suffering from communicable disease are permitted to travel by plane.
The overnight train stop at Penticton, with consequent moving of stretcher cases and considerable
Interim Supply
delay in reaching the desired medical attention at the coast is also a serious factor.
The board of directors fully appreciates the difficulties under which train service is maintained in this area, but feels it is their duty to point out the serious inadequacies of the present drastically curtailed service when sick persons require transportation.
It is asked that you give this matter your considered attention and do all in your power to press for improved rail passenger service for Nelson.
Yours truly,
E. M. Stiles, Chairman of the Board
That deals with the passenger train service, Mr. Chairman, which lacks sleeping car and refreshment car accommodation. Under present circumstances, owing to certain actions on the part of certain persons unknown at the present time, the service has been somewhat curtailed between Vancouver and Nelson although, I understand, at the wish of the attorney general of British Columbia. The men operating on the road cannot understand why it is possible to run freight trains daily and yet it is not possible to run a passenger train daily. However, I am not going to deal with that aspect of the question because it is one that is somewhat unusual and somewhat abnormal. But we are concerned about this running of a Budd car over this long length of railway through our territory.
When the Minister of Transport was in Nelson and peregrinating around my constituency during the election he was met by representatives of the municipal council, trade unions, chambers of commerce and other organizations. In conversation with them I understand he admitted he had no power under the act to compel the Canadian Pacific railway to improve the service. I am sure the former minister of transport will correct me if I am incorrect in this. This is a reduction of service and it does not impose upon the company the necessity to ask the board of transport commissioners for permission. On that basis you can reduce it to almost zero and still not contravene the act. I am of the opinion that there should be an amendment to the act in that respect, and I intend to introduce a private bill, when we get over the first hurried days of the session, suggesting an amendment of that type.
The minister did say that he would-and as I indicated yesterday this was his political trump on that occasion-consult with Messrs. Crump and Rump. Apparently he has not been very successful. In his answer to my question yesterday he rather indicated to me that the matter has been sort of satisfactorily settled. I think there has been some improvement with respect to the handling of express, some livestock and things of that

Interim Supply
sort. The basic complaint still rests there and that is why I am rising today at the request of the people whom I have mentioned. I do not think these people are asking too much. We recognize the difficulties. You cannot ask people to run trains for nothing, without patronage and things of that sort. The patronage is diminishing daily because of the nature of the service. I do urge the minister to do everything in his power, to go into this matter again with the appropriate officials of the Canadian Pacific railway, to see whether this train could not also include a sleeping car and a dining car or a cafe car. If the train consisted of a sleeping car, a cafe car and a coach, the service of the district would be improved and there would be comfort there for old people, people with families, mentally and physically ill people and for the public generally.
I have said all I wish to say at this time, Mr. Chairman. I made these few remarks at the request, as I said before, of a large number of organizations and in support of the opinions of 100 per cent of the people who reside in southeastern British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, in presenting his budgetary statement on December 6 the Minister of Finance said that he would accept the former minister's estimates of income and in spite of further proposed principal expenditures he expected a budgetary surplus of $106 million. Can the minister tell the committee whether those figures now stand? If not, what was the situation at the end of the 1957-58 budgetary year?
I would expect the minister to be approximately right in his predictions because they were made after two-thirds of the fiscal year had passed; but it is right that we should know something about the past year before we appropriate money for this year. On December 6 the minister predicted savings in deductions of $64 million. Yesterday I thought he mentioned that this amounted to $73.6 million. I should like to ask him what these savings were.
I have heard the minister on many occasions refer to the waste and extravagance of former governments, when the Hon. Mr. Harris and the Hon. Mr. Abbott were ministers of finance. I think he made these criticisms more in the light of the fact that the estimates were up in those particular years. This year, if one looks over the estimates that were tabled on Tuesday, one finds a substantial increase in almost every department. I know that the estimates of the Department of National Defence have decreased by $6.8 million. It is also true
[Mr. Herridge.l
that the minister's own department shows a decrease in expenditure of $18 million, but his department benefits to the extent of over $100 million as a result of the change in the federal-provincial tax sharing agreement with the province of Ontario. If we took all those tax sharing agreements and totalled them up I calculate that he would have an increase in expenditure of $31 million in his department instead of a decrease of $18 million.
In the past I have heard the minister refer to the large number of civil servants as an example of waste and extravagance. Last year the former secretary of state, during the consideration of her estimates, admitted to me that the number of civil servants was up over the preceding year. I should like to ask the minister if he has been successful in effecting a reduction in the number of civil servants this year.
There has been an increase of over $6.5 million in interest alone on our public debt. This is shown in these estimates. This represents an increase of about 40 cents for every man, woman and child in Canada. I feel that this is only the beginning. It suggests to me that the poor old taxpayer in Canada is going to have a tough time in the years ahead. Being told by the Minister of Finance the charges on the public debt does not inform us of the amount of the public debt itself and this, in my opinion, is unprecedented. I believe that he must know the debt in order to calculate the interest on it, and he should reveal the amount at this time.
In any event this house should be favoured with a statement on the 1957-58 budgetary year before we vote money for the current fiscal year. As the people's representatives we have been kept in the dark long enough. Any government which respects the rights of parliament and the rights of the people should tell us how we stood at the end of the last fiscal year before asking us to vote money for this fiscal year. They should not leave so much to surmise. We should be able to obtain a clear idea concerning how much this government is spending to run our country, and we should also be told how much the unemployment insurance fund has been depleted since they took office last June.

I wonder if the minister would be good enough to repeat his answer. The loud speaker system does not seem to be working properly and no one heard his reply concerning a contemplated dominion-municipal conference.

I notice the minister of mines is in the house, and I wonder if he would answer a question which has something to do with the supply that would be passed for his department? Representations have been made by the geologists association of Canada that some emergency steps be taken by his department with regard to the employment of undergraduates who are training as geologists. I wonder if the minister could give me any information on that?
