subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Starr (Minister of Labour) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the temporary extension of the seasonal

benefit periods under the Unemployment Insurance Act for a six weeks period, from May 18, 1958, to June 28, 1958.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sevigny in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this bill is to extend the six weeks period from May 17 to June 28 as the period in which seasonal benefits may be paid. We are proposing a life span of only six weeks for this legislation because it is intended to meet a situation which we believe will not recur.
As hon. members know, unemployment reached a postwar high during last winter and while the situation has considerably and markedly improved in recent weeks there still exists something of a special problem in that there remain people in our labour force who need further protection pending a firmer upturn in economic activity. We believe this upturn is now in evidence and that is why we are at this time proposing this short-term legislation which will, without disrupting the existing formula, provide the flexibility we need to meet this particular set of circumstances.
This measure will place additional purchasing power in the hands of those who most need it. We estimate that some 200,000 claimants will benefit from this legislation to the extent of close to $14 million. I would like to note that in the five months beginning December 1, 1957, and I think this will answer a question asked in the house earlier, almost $230 million were paid out in unemployment insurance benefits but in spite of these heavy expenditures the unemployment insurance fund had at the end of March a remarkably healthy balance of more than $740 million. We feel that this fund is therefore in a sound position to yield this extra protection which we feel should be provided and thus continue to do the job it was intended to do.
In further explanation of this bill I would like to emphasize both what it is proposed to do and what it is not proposed to do. Perhaps for the benefit of those who are not familiar with our unemployment legislation I could best begin by explaining what seasonal benefit is and also its relation to regular benefit.
Seasonal benefit was brought into being in 1950 after a decade of experience with unemployment insurance which had revealed two weaknesses in the regular benefit formula. Firstly, there was a large number of Canadian workers who simply did not work long enough each year in insurable employment to ever be able to qualify for regular benefits and, secondly, there were many whose
Unemployment Insurance regular benefits became exhausted during the winter months, the very time when it was most difficult to get another job. The seasonal benefit idea was to lower the normal qualifying requirements for a limited period and thus provide unemployed workers with a better bridge with which to span the gap between jobs, a gap that was causing a good deal of hardship to many Canadians through the years.
Last autumn we improved the structure of this bridge when we lengthened the seasonal benefit period by one month at each end. Where it was previously from January 1 to April 15 we extended it to from December 1 to May 15 and now we are proposing another temporary improvement to meet a special situation.
I would like to make it quite clear at this time that this bill does not constitute a blanket addition of six weeks of benefits for those who are now drawing seasonal benefits and I must emphasize that benefit payments also have to be based on prior contributions, but it does mean that those who have not exhausted all their entitlement by May 17 will be able to go on drawing benefits until they do exhaust their entitlement, or until June 28. But for this legislation all seasonal benefit payments would, of course, cease on May 17, this week.
Perhaps a few examples will help to illustrate the categories of claimants who will be entitled to additional protection from this measure. Let us take persons who became unemployed early in February. Those claimants had 24 contributions since the previous March 31-that is, March 31, 1957-and on the basis of five weeks of benefits for every six weeks of contributions they were able to qualify for 20 weeks of seasonal benefits, effective February 9. Under the present legislation payments to these claimants would cease on May 17 even though they had used up only 14 of their possible 20 weeks. The bill we are proposing will enable them to go on drawing the other six weeks of their entitlement. Thus, he receives his full 20 weeks to which he is entitled because of his contribution.
Another category of claims which will benefit from the legislation affects those who become unemployed and who claim benefit on or about May 17 but who are unable to qualify for regular benefit. Such claims could under this measure be considered for seasonal benefit provided the claimant had not already exhausted the seasonal benefits claimed since December 1, 1957. Under the present legislation there would be no possibility of qualifying for seasonal benefit on failure to qualify for regular benefit because this benefit period would end this week on May 17.

Unemployment Insurance
A third example would be a claimant who earlier in the year had been drawing seasonal benefit but who had found work again before exhausting all his entitlement. Suppose he becomes unemployed again. Under present legislation he would be unable to draw his unused entitlement because the seasonal benefit period would be over on May 17. Under this bill, however, he would be able to receive payment either until his entitlement was used up or until June 28. With this example I think it would be clear that claimants who would not be entitled to further payment as a result of this legislation are those who have already been paid all the seasonal benefit to which they are entitled. A claimant who earlier established his right to 20 weeks seasonal benefit and who has already been paid 20 weeks seasonal benefit will not receive further payment and, as I have noted, benefit is based on prior contributions.
There are two other small points I should like to note in regard to this bill. One is that no waiting period would have to be served in respect to these additional weeks established as a result of this extension. The other is that this bill applies equally to those engaged in the fishing industry who were covered this year for the first time by special regulations under the act.
In conclusion I should like to say again that this bill is a temporary bill designed to solve a temporary problem. It is, in fact, a re-affirmation of an aim we have often enunciated, namely that Canadian workers shall not suffer hardships because of unemployment that occurs through no fault of their own.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister who has just spoken said that this particular measure was one designed to cover a situation which-to use his own language-he believed would not occur again. I am sure all of us in this house would agree with the minister in hoping that the situation which brought this bill into being will not occur again. However, the Prime Minister, when he spoke yesterday, said at the conclusion of his speech as reported on page 42 of Hansard:
First, we meet the problem of unemployment by again removing the difficulties inherent in the extension of the payments.
He was referring to the measure which has just been introduced by the hon. minister. I am sure the minister himself will be the first to recognize that this particular measure does not in any way meet the problem of unemployment. This is an amendment designed to give assistance to men and women in our country who are without work and


who need financial assistance in order to maintain themselves and their families. In no circumstances can anyone be justified in saying, as the Prime Minister observed yesterday, that this is a measure designed, to use his own words again, to meet the problem of unemployment. The fact is that the measure before us does not touch the problem of unemployment except in the way I have mentioned.
We are therefore obliged to bring to the attention of the government at this time, as was done by my leader yesterday, the fact that the foremost domestic problem in Canada at this moment is that there are about six hundred thousand men and women out of work. This does represent a very serious situation and the government, having the responsibility, has a definite obligation to give leadership in this matter, a leadership which, if it is given, will be warmly supported, I am sure, by every hon. member in this house who shares the view of the Prime Minister expressed during the election that unemployment was a social disaster.
The fact that the unemployment insurance fund lost $131 million in the last fiscal year and-if my estimate is correct-a further $40 million in April, 1958, is in itself an indication of the seriousness of unemployment in our country. An examination of the statement of revenues and expenditures of the unemployment insurance fund over the period of the last two months spells out in an emphatic way the extent of this problem in Canada. I have before me certain reported expenditures by way of benefit payments through supplementary and seasonal benefits provided under the amendment of last fall. I find that in the month of December last the total supplementary and seasonal benefits paid out were $2 million. In the month of January they rose to $12 million-I am now using round figures-in the month of February to $15 million, and in the month of March last to almost $20 million. Those are figures having to do with supplementary and seasonal payments.
The situation is even more serious when examined in the light of the total benefit payments including supplementary and seasonal payments as well as ordinary payments provided for under the Unemployment Insurance Act. For instance, in the month of September last it was $13 million; in October, $16 million; in the month of November, $18 million, close to $19 million; in the month of December, $31 million, close to $32 million; in the month of January, $60 million; in the month of February, $63 million and in the month of March, $72 million. Again I use round figures.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I draw to the attention of the hon. member who is now quoting these figures that he is taking the ordinary column, say, in the month of December, amounting to $29 million and then adding the total to it to make it $60 million. Actually, he should be taking the ordinary figure of $29 million and adding to it the supplementary figure of $2 million to get $31 million.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext: My hon. friend could be correct but he will not deny that the figure for-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
Some hon. members applaud but I am sure they have not fully appreciated the point the minister has made. The fact is that the figure for the month of March is some $72 million and my hon. friend will remember that in the month of February last year I suggested to him that the estimates which I had made at that time based upon the figures then presented suggest that the total expenditures could reach the figure of same $73 million at the end of March of this year. The report now indicates that this is the situation.
These figures in themselves reflect the seriousness of the problem in Canada. It does not mean, of course, that the jobless figures are identical with the implications involved in these figures but it does indicate that at the present time the unemployment problem in Canada continues to be an extremely serious one. I suggest it is the first and most important problem on the domestic level facing Canada and the government and parliament at this time.
This particular measure is not in any way going to relieve the pressure or improve the situation. The government, along with the other factors in the Canadian economy and the Canadian people, will have to resort to measures other than this if the government is going to be able to say it has made some serious reduction in the level of unemployment in Canada.
In 1955 when we had a situation not comparable to this, but one in which there were a lot of people out of work and when the then minister of labour proposed measures of this sort, hon. members opposite were insistent in reminding the government of that day that with regard to unemployment it had a highly important and direct obligation. The present Minister of Transport, for instance, said in 1955, and his words can be found on page 76 of Hansard for that year:
Unemployment Insurance
Despite this evidence, however, the government seems to persist-well, it does not 'seem', it persists-simply to duck its responsibilities in this matter, so far as the citizens of Canada are concerned.
The hon. gentleman was talking about unemployment, as the context of his remarks will show. I suggest to the government today that those words of the Minister of Transport are much more applicable now than they were then. The same is true of the words of the distinguished new Minister of Citizenship and Immigration as found at page 138 of Hansard for 1955 when she said:
They-
The unemployedcannot live even on 100 per cent-
-of regular benefits. While I do not want to comment on the fairness of that characterization I say to the minister if those words were applicable then they are certainly applicable today. Nobody can live on even 100 per cent of seasonal benefits and certainly these benefits in themselves will not provide work for men and women who need it.
In my own community of Windsor, as the Minister of Labour knows, there are still many thousands of men and women out of work as there are all over this country. Inasmuch as this measure will assist some it will be welcomed, but the fact is, and the country should know it, this amendment will not assist the majority of the unemployed in Canada.
We also have the statement of the present Minister of Transport in 1955, as reported at page 143 of Hansard, when he said:
There is no use in the minister saying the government is doing everything it can. I say that everything you can do is not being done. You are trying to find them jobs, but you cannot find them jobs. A man finds himself without credits and without a job. He has a family and he has to eat, and so does his family. What are you going to do for him? I want to know that.
That, too, is the question which I know the Minister of Labour for whom I have the greatest respect will understand is in the minds of many thousands of men and women throughout Canada as well as in the minds of hon. members of this house as we begin the discussion of this matter.
What we should have from the government is a clear statement indicating what steps it proposes to take if it believes it can take steps to relieve this situation. We know the difficulties involved but yesterday we were given the impression by the Prime Minister that the government was tackling this problem and that the bottom had been reached. However there is no real evidence before this house that the bottom of unemployment in Canada has been reached.

Unemployment Insurance There is evidence to the contrary and we have good reasons for suspecting that in a period when unemployment should be somewhat reduced we are likely to find increased unemployment, that is during the months of July and August. It is estimated, I understand, that possibly as many as 300,000 people will be out of work at that time.
This government has not yet presented us with a program by which this problem could be resolved. I suggest that at this stage the government might well look at the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition when speaking about this matter during the course of the federal election on February 12 when he said:
In order to provide special incentives for work to be carried on in the winter months whenever possible, a Liberal government would set an example to private enterprise and to provincial and local governments by recognizing that winter joblessness is a real cost to the community and it is therefore sound economics to carry on some kinds of work even though they are more expensive in the winter. Whenever appropriate, therefore, we would provide in federal contracts the payment of adequate extra costs where work is done in the winter; and we would oiler effective grants in aid to the municipalities and local authorities to enable them to do the same.
I mention that as the kind of approach the government could take as a means of dealing with this problem. What have we been told in that connection? We were told by the Prime Minister that a program of public works could do the job. No one will deny that a properly conceived program of public works could put a considerable number of men and women in this country to work but certainly not the program enunciated by the Prime Minister just prior to the last general election, one which is not in fact a public works program at all. That has been said repeatedly but this is the place now to examine it and to unmask this synthetic and alleged program of public works.
I ask the government to tell us during the course of this debate how many men and women have been put to work as a result of the operation of this public works program to date? How many men and women will be put to work as a result of the expenditure of $1,185 million during the course of the present fiscal year? How many men were put to work as a result of the expenditure for three months of some $270 million involved in this program which was announced with all of the powerful propaganda available to the government at the beginning of this election?
When we examine this program we find it is not an emergency program at all. The program announced by the Prime Minister represented items that had been for the most

part contained in the estimates of the previous administration. It included the St. Lawrence seaway representing $106 million; the Canadian National railways, $140 million; the Department of Public Works, $145 million; national harbours board, $38 million; Department of Transport, $244 million; Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, $308 million; and crown corporations, $72 million.
All of these items are the ordinary annual estimates for the departments or the crown corporations I have named. They are not materially different from those tabled by the former administration for 1957. In fact, they come surprisingly close to the same figure so that we on this side of the house say with confidence that that particular program of public works, designed to relieve unemployment, could not possibly have been used for that purpose. If hon. gentlemen opposite disagree, I ask them to tell us how many individuals, in addition to those normally engaged in those particular enterprises of the crown, have been employed as a result of the enunciation of this policy. If the answer is not to be given or if it is in the negative, what steps does the government propose to take to try and do something about this problem of unemployment?
There are many things that the government can do, and about some of those I would like to say something in a few moments. I suggest to the Minister of Labour, who carries this measure for the government at this time, that he and the government should give very careful consideration to the proposal made by the Leader of the Opposition, a proposal which is being seriously examined in the United States, where they likewise have a problem which, in terms of unemployment, is not quite as serious as ours. I might say to the Minister of Labour one thing he could do that would help some in my own constituency, as I am sure it would help in his, is to abolish completely, for instance, the tax on automobiles. That would help considerably. There are many other things the government could do. I am not placing this on the doorstep of the Minister of Labour alone because it is a responsibility that belongs to the government as a whole. In spite of its boasts, in spite of the mandate given to it by the people of Canada, this government has not given any evidence of a program designed to meet this national problem of unemployment in Canada at this time.
I have said that the particular measure before us, commendable to the extent that it goes, does not in any way provide assistance to anything like a substantial proportion of those individuals who are now in receipt of unemployment insurance or whose benefits

are running out. I do not know what the exact figure is of those who are on unemployment benefits at this time, but I suggest to the Minister of Labour that this particular measure will not give assistance to a quarter of the men and women who are now in receipt of unemployment insurance. I suggest further that there will be great disappointment that the extension contemplated in this measure will not include those whose benefits run out prior to May 17. If that is the situation-and I understood the Minister of Labour to indicate that that was the situation-this extension will actually only benefit those who have any credits on May 17, or who have been able to file a claim for seasonal periods following their regular benefit period. If this is the situation, and I believe it is, I am sure the minister will appreciate that there will be great disappointment in the country.
I think we should have a clear statement on this point from the minister so that we can get a true appreciation of this amendment which, in so far as providing assistance to individuals who come within its compass are concerned, will be welcomed by us. We should not underestimate the help provided nor should we exaggerate the benefits proposed. I would ask the minister to tell us at some point in our discussion how many persons have established seasonal benefit claims for the period from December 1, 1957 to May 15, 1958. I would also like to ask him what was the aggregate amount of seasonal benefits paid to such persons. We would be able to derive some impression of this particular measure if we get from the minister the answers that he should be able to give us. I know he will give us answers but I suggest to him-I know he does not want to mislead the public or this house; he is not that kind of man-that he should give us a clear and concise statement indicating precisely what the cost of this is going to be. Is it going to be $9 million; is it going to be $14 million; is it going to be $30 million? From this answer we shall be able to make a deduction as to the likely number of individuals who, at
Unemployment Insurance least in part, will get some assistance from the amendment proposed in the resolution before the house.
I submit to the minister that those are very important considerations if we are to discharge our responsibility in this matter. As the minister said, the Unemployment Insurance Act-introduced, incidentally, by another administration in 1940-was amended in 1950 to provide for the first time for the payment of supplementary benefits during the period of January 1 to March 31. As my hon. friend said, advantage was taken of the experience of the operation of the act to deal with this particular traditional mid-winter problem which we have in Canada, though abnormally greater this year.
Four classes of seasonal benefit payments were established by the 1950 amendment. For a proper understanding of the measure before us we should clearly understand what those four classes were. We should also recognize the importance of maintaining the integrity of the unemployment insurance fund which is contributed to mainly by two groups of the Canadian people, the employee and the employer, with a smaller contribution by the people as a whole through the government. It is a fund to which a limited number of Canadian citizens contribute; it is a fund, the integrity of which we wish to see maintained. The time has come when we should carefully examine this situation in the light of this important objective.
Progress reported.
